message.content: I've analyzed the bisection-threshold kernel against the lenient-tie contract. The key structural risk: the `count >= K` invariant protects kept>=dropped ordering, but nothing forces the converged `lo` to actually sit at the k-th cutoff — it can land strictly below the k-th largest value, admitting entries that are strictly below the k-th largest (not tied at the cutoff), which both readings of the contract disallow. Plus two k-domain edge cases.

function.arguments: {"rationale": "The bisection keeps `lo` at the highest mid whose count(x>=mid)>=K, but after only 40 halvings the bracket width is (hi-lo)/2^40; with large-magnitude or ULP-close scores (e.g. values ~1e20 whose gaps are smaller than the residual bracket), lo can end strictly between the (k+1)-th and k-th largest values, and keep=(x>=lo) then admits entries strictly below the k-th largest — not tied at the cutoff — changing downstream renormalized weights.", "scope": "in_scope", "scope_evidence": [{"source": "problem.txt", "summary": "out[j] = scores[j] only 'if scores[j] is among the k largest of the row'; the lenient tie clause covers only entries sharing the value at the k-th position — an entry strictly below the k-th largest is neither among the k largest nor tied at the cutoff, so admitting it violates the stated contract. No input magnitude bounds restrict scores, so scores with close gaps are admitted inputs."}], "statement": "For rows where the gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th largest values is smaller than the residual bisection bracket (~range*2^-40) but the values are distinct (e.g. large-magnitude float scores), topk_mask keeps entries strictly below the k-th largest value that are not tied at the cutoff, producing a kept set larger than k under either contract reading."}

message.reasoning_content:
Record claims. The most promising: 40-iteration bisection may admit more than intended? The kept>=dropped invariant should hold given the count>=K invariant... actually the invariant protects it: lo always satisfies count(x>=lo)>=K, so keep set has >= K elements and everything dropped is < lo <= kept values. That's safe. The real bug risk: bisection doesn't converge to exact cutoff — keep may include MORE than the tie cluster? No: keep = x >= lo, and lo <= true k-th value cutoff? count(x>=lo)>=K means at least K entries >= lo; all dropped < lo. So invariant holds. Only edge cases k=0 and k>N break. Also potential lo==hi convergence: mid = (lo+hi)*0.5; if hi-lo shrinks below float precision, mid could equal lo or hi... fine.

One subtle bug: initial hi = tl.max(x) where invalid lanes are -inf, fine. But if all values are -inf... edge.

Better concrete in-scope claim: bisection admits values below the k-th value when the bracket doesn't fully converge — keep = x >= lo, and lo can be strictly below the k-th largest value by residual bracket width. Wait, if lo < kth value, then count(x>=lo) >= K still, and everything below lo dropped. But entries between lo and kth value are kept? No — keep = x >= lo, so entries with value in [lo, kth) are kept even though they're below the k-th largest. Then dropped entries are < lo, kept entries >= lo. Is that a contract violation? "every kept entry is at least as large as every dropped one" — still satisfied! But "out[j]=scores[j] if among the k largest" — keeping more than k non-tied entries means keeping entries that are strictly smaller than some dropped? No, dropped ones are < lo. Hmm, but keeping more than k entries where ties do NOT exist at the cutoff would mean keeping entries strictly below the k-th largest — that violates "among the k largest" and downstream renormalization gives nonzero weight to non-top-k entries. This is the real claim: if bisection's final lo lands strictly between the (k+1)-th and k-th distinct values... wait no, if lo in (k+1th value, kth value), count(x>=lo) = K exactly only if no values in [lo, kth). Since lo < kth value and count(x>=lo)>=K, values between lo and kth would add to count. If lo < kth value then all K top values >= lo, count >= K. If there are values in (lo, kth), they're kept though below kth largest — kept set > K without ties. Contract violation? The contract says tied entries only admitted at the cutoff; keeping strictly-lower entries that aren't among the k largest is a violation of "keep the top-k... zero the rest" and would change downstream renormalized weights. This happens when 40 iterations don't fully separate the gap. With float32 and 40 halvings, gap shrinks by 2^40 ≈ 1e12, so relative gaps > 1e-12 relative converge fine. But gaps smaller than ~2^-40 * range could fail — e.g., values differing by ULP. But then they're near-ties... hmm, near-tie small gaps could be argued either way. Actually with floats, values differing by 1 ULP at magnitude 1e30 would have gaps that 40 halvings can't resolve (2^-40*1e30 >> ULP). So claim: with large-magnitude scores with distinct-but-close values, the kernel keeps extra entries below the k-th largest, violating the "keep only top-k" rule (no ties at cutoff). Is large-magnitude in scope? No input bounds — scope unknown/arguable. problem.txt doesn't bound magnitudes, so in_scope per "contract is whatever artifact states"? Magnitudes aren't excluded. I'll mark in_scope citing problem.txt formula (top-k only) but note gap condition.

Second claim: k > n_cols keeps everything — including entries not among top-k; also k=0 keeps max entries. Scope: k bounds unspecified; unknown.

Third: BLOCK — n_cols not power of 2 handled by mask, fine.

I'll record 3 claims: (1) bisection under-separation keeps non-top-k entries; (2) k=0 keeps max-valued entries instead of nothing; (3) k>N keeps all entries. Scope: unknown for 2,3; 1 in_scope with problem.txt evidence.
